He said: "We have decided to use as high as 40 per cent lignite." Then he went on to say that they would use as high as 80 per cent lignite. Of two things one is certain. When these people come forward promising, as the minister himself stated the other night they had promised, that they will burn up to 80 per cent lignite, either all the objections they have urged against the use of lignite go by the board, or else they are not bona fide in their promise. It must be one or the other. Either all their objections go by the board, or they do not intend to carry out their promise. I suppose there is another possibility; that they are not limited to those two horns of the dilemma. It may be that the two alternatives I have named are both correct; one thing is certainly true that they have not been bona fide throughout.
In order that lignite coal may be burned in the manner I have described it is mixed with bituminous coal. What does that mean? It means that they would add the expense of mixing probably 100,000 tons of coal by hand, shovelful by shovelful, in order to get a good mix. All that just adds to the expense; and instead of making the saving that they otherwise could have made by using lignite coal, that saving will be to a considerable extent wiped out by this additional labour which they will deliberately bring into play. If they could save money by using up to 80 per cent, why cannot they save by using lignite up to 100 per cent?
The only people who mix bituminous and lignite coal are those who do it under circumstances such as these, for instance. There is, in Winnipeg, a large central heating plant, one of the really large ones of the country, but they put in their equipment originally to bum bituminous coal before this lignite coal had such an established place on the market. Then lignite coal came on the market and they found that anyone burning lignite got his steam cheaper. These people had to find some way to cut their costs; while it was not satisfactory to bum a mixture of lignite and bituminous in the equipment they already had, nevertheless they went ahead and mixed the two coals because they could save a little money that way, and then, as finances would permit, they would switch from the equipment they had bought originally until they had the new type of equipment entirely. They are making that switch unit by unit. Every time they make a switch they get the new equipment for burning lignite coal, and by that method they are saving a great deal of money as fast as they can.
An industrialist sometimes finds himself in the position of burning bituminous and of see-

ing a competitor put in new equipment and burning lignite coal. He cannot himself change over immediately, and so he mixes the coal in order to try to keep up with his competitor. It is only in such circumstances that these two kinds of coal are mixed. Everybody else naturally keeps away from mixing the two coals.
But these people-Allied War Supplies Corporation-are proposing to mix the coal. They finally come to promise that, when people put pressure on them. I go back to the statement I made before either that this promise which they are now making, under pressure, to burn lignite coal is not a bona fide one, or, if it is, it wipes out every objection they have ever made to the burning of lignite coal. Probably both these propositions are correct.
In support of what some people have said, I should like to read an editorial on the subject; an editorial not particularly in my favour. The Winnipeg Free Press, dealing with the question wrote under date of March 13, what I think everybody will admit is a sound editorial. It said:
The big chemical plant being erected east of Winnipeg will use a very large amount of coal, and the question of the type of coal that should be used has been raised. It is understood that the installation of equipment for the use of bituminous coal is contemplated, although it is well known in business circles here that that type of stoker has been increasingly replaced in recent years in this city by equipment for using the cheaper lignite coal. The economy is so great that the change has been made, or is being gradually made, by nearly all large users of coal in this district.
This equipment costs more than that for using bituminous coal, but the difference is a matter of dispute, and what it would be in the case of the chemical plant is for experts to say, as is the question of the relation between that difference and the saving through the use of lignite.
That is as far as I need read. I wanted to quote that last sentence, that it is a question for the experts to decide. I do not think anyone would disagree with that, generally speaking, as a sound piece of advice. But here is the picture to keep in mind regarding the experts. Last January or last February I wrote to the Minister of Munitions and Supply about this matter, telling him that the present situation ought to be guarded against.	I
know that he dealt with the matter. I also know that at that time he was extremely busy because it was just after he had returned from overseas, and when he inquired into the matter I have no doubt that certain things were told him which caused him not to look into it any further. As a matter of fact, he must have been dealing with it back about January because about that time Wharton

War Appropriation Bill
wrote the letter that I have read to the committee. In spite of that letter, in spite of what may have been said between the minister and Mr. Crabtree, in spite of the decisions they may have made, Mr. Crabtree told a colleague of mine in this house on or about February 25 that this question was still open, that they were approaching it with a completely open mind. Then two days later, after the engineer wrote, his man Abbott told me and that same colleague that he could not understand how Crabtree could have said that; that Crabtree knew the facts; that this matter was settled long ago, definitely settled beyond being raised again, and that he could not understand how Mr. Crabtree could have made that statement. In spite of the fact that Wharton wrote to the effect that lignite could not be used, Abbott told us in that interview that they were going to use lignite to the extent of somewhere between 40 and 80 per cent. I could not help feeling, as I still feel, that there is something pretty rotten in the whole situation. When I reviewed a set of facts like that, I could not help feeling that these people were being a great deal less than frank.
The same story is in the correspondence I read to the committee. The representative of the fuel board deals with these people and apparently finds them intractable. He takes the matter up with the prices board, and they arrange to write a strong letter on the subject so as, in any event, to put themselves on record. They do so, and they give cogent reasons why these people should use lignite. It is in accordance with government policy that they should do so, because it is in accordance with government policy to save fuel and rolling stock. Even then Mr. Crabtree says, "We are giving consideration yet to that matter." By inference, from the letter I read, there is still an "open door." It was not until about a week or so ago that I learned definitely, conclusively, and, one might say, for the last time, that Crabtree's engineers are apparently "already"-that is the expression-"too far committed." If that is not the story of an irresponsible organization playing ducks and drakes with you, then you tell one.
They are not too far committed, Mr Chairman, to do what is right. They must be made to do it. They can get the equipment. If they have already ordered their other equipment, they can do one of two things. They can take it and sell it at some loss, or they can cancel the order and pay some loss. The savings will more than make up for any loss so incurred. Indeed, that is one of the points they make, that this other equipment they have ordered has salvage value. They 14873-104
can get something for it. Well, let them get something for it; it will have all the more salvage value if they dispose of it now while it is new. Let this organization, however, now do what is right with reference to the policy of the government of Canada and show a proper regard for the money of the people of the old country which we have in trust.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think it is
a fair summary of the hon. member's remarks that he said that something very uneconomical is being done in designing this cordite plant. I see no point of order there. If the cordite plant is economically designed-and I think we must assume that the people responsible are designing it to the best of their ability-* we can reasonably assume that the remarks which my hon. friend has made, taking over three hours of the time of the committee, are themselves very much out of order. Either the plant as at present designed is economical, or it is not.
As I have said, the problem at Winnipeg is not to build something for the burning of a certain type of coal. That is incidental to the problem. The problem is to build an explosives plant. I know something about building plants for a special purpose. I have spent all my life at such work. I know that in building a grain elevator there are certain practices which, although they do very well for other industries, are not economic when applied to a grain elevator; and the power part is very much a case in point. People have accepted my judgment with regard to the matter because I had the reputation of being able successfully to build grain elevators.
Similarly, when we are building an explosives plant we go to people who have a reputation for being able to build, successfully and economically, explosives plants. I may say that two explosives plants built by this organization, Allied War Supplies, with their experts, Defence Industries Limited, are in operation and producing cordite cheaper than any other plant on this continent. That, I think, is something to the credit of those responsible for the operation.
The production of explosives has several peculiarities which it is well to note at this stage. One of them is that the dangers from explosives are related very closely to the degree of cleanliness which is maintained in a plant. Those hon. members who have ever visited an explosives plant know that before you pass into the operational part of it you are required to take off your shoes, to go over the operational part bare-footed, or to put on other shoes which are furnished to you and which are never allowed to pass out of the explosives part of the plant. So much for cleanliness, and I might say that practically every explosion which occurs in an

explosives plant is caused by carelessness on the part of the workmen, in allowing something unclean to develop in the plant, permitting dirt to accumulate, or cordite or some other explosive to drop on the floor from a barrel or some other receptacle.
The problem of cleanliness is definitely related to the coal supply. It is reported in the correspondence that pulverized coal cannot be used on account of the danger of sparks and the dust resulting from the coal. It is true that lignite is a cheap coal, very economical for certain purposes; but it is also true that to get the same amount of heat from lignite as from Alberta bituminous coal, twice the volume has to be burned. It is also well known that lignite will not stand storage particularly. It breaks down quickly to slack coal, much more quickly than does Alberta coal; and it is known further that lignite in the slack form, that is, the dust of lignite, has the same objections that pulverized coal of any kind has, in that it is a distributor of dust and ash.
The problem, I know-it is obvious from the record-was thoroughly studied, because every possible pressure was brought to bear upon the company to use lignite. Those responsible for the sale of lignite have, in my opinion, exhausted every possibility that could be thought of, including pressure upon the fuel controller, and that part has been quite thoroughly done. Knowing these facts, the board of directors of Allied War Supplies Corporation have still come to the conclusion that the course they are pursuing is the proper one. Nothing could have been overlooked in the matter, because it is obvious from the record that every fact in connection with the problem was brought to their attention.
Someone may ask, what do you know about the problem? I know very little about it. I was in Europe when it was being discussed. I went to England, having left Ottawa on December 4, and I returned to Canada in the last few days of January. The matter was called to my attention then by the same agencies that have raised it in the house, and I called Mr. Crabtree to Ottawa, or at least asked him to discuss the matter with me on the first occasion on which he was in Ottawa. He came with a technical expert, and we discussed the relative merits of lignite coal and bituminous coal for that locality. We discussed the matter for the best part of an hour, and in that time Mr. Crabtree reviewed all the facts that had been presented to him and gave the reasons why he had come to the conclusion that the equipment being installed was the proper equipment for the purpose. As I said in the house

War Appropriation Bill
earlier, he did not close the door upon burning a portion of lignite in the grates, and the reason for that is that if coal can be transferred direct from the cars under the boilers, there is not the same danger from dust that there is if the coal has to be stored for a time. I pointed out to him at the time, however, that it seemed desirable to use coal from the lignite field, if only from the point of view of coal conservation. He said he agreed with me entirely and it was their intention to do the best they could in that direction, but there were limits beyond which, in his judgment, they could not go. After the study which I knew he had given the matter; after the expert type of opinion which I knew he would obtain, I saw no reason for pursuing the matter further.
A forum has been set up in which this matter can be properly considered, namely, the committee on economy. The advantage of that committee is that Mr. Crabtree can be there and refute any statements such as the ex parte statements made in this house. His experts can be brought before that committee. The Estevan coal people can bring their experts, and the committee can decide the case with the fullest possible technical information before them.
I suppose that if I had time I could make myself sufficiently familiar with all the facts in this case to discuss each item that has been taken up by the hon. member. Frankly, however, I have not the time to do it. I have gone into the matter sufficiently to satisfy myself that every factor was taken into account, that expert opinion was brought to bear on it, and that the action taken by Allied War Supplies Corporation followed the advice of their expert opinion. I may say that these were not street-corner opinions. They were the opinions of men who were paid to give their expert advice on the problem. They were the opinions of men who were qualified, by success in fuel engineering, to give advice. I know that the advice of the national research laboratories was brought to bear on the problem, as it is on all problems involving coal purchased by the Department of Munitions and Supply or by any officers responsible to that department. I know that this opinion was available to Allied War Supplies Corporation and that it was used accordingly.
That is all I wish to say on the matter. It is not my duty to say to the committee on economy what cases they should hear or when they should hear them, but I express the opinion that it is desirable that the committee should see whether economies were overlooked in this particular case, having in view the exacting requirements in connection with the manufacture of explosives. If the
committee, after examining into the situation, report to the house that there has been failure to carry out economy in the transaction, even though it is wholly for the British government, I shall be glad to take corrective steps at that time.

I do not desire at this stage of the proceedings or at this late hour of the afternoon to enter into any part of the controversy between the minister and one of his followers; but there is a larger aspect, with respect to the establishment and situation of this cordite plant, to which I direct attention for a few moments. Why was this plant located 2,000 miles from seaboard?
I have made some investigation. We have, according to the minister's statement, a commitment of something over $9,000,000, all for the account of the United Kingdom, and I understand the plant is to be increased substantially, so that before this plant is finally completed and in full operation there will have been a capital expenditure of between $13,000,000 and $14,000,000. That is a great deal of money.
The raw materials for cordite are four. First, there is cotton lintos, which is the odds and ends of cotton. This is imported from the United States and is, of course, as easily available to Winnipeg as to a site on seaboard. I understand that plans are under way to make use of wood pulp in substitution for cotton.
The second ingredient in the manufacture of cordite is nitric acid, which is made at each explosive plant from ammonia. At the present time there is a contract for the supply of ammonia from the United States. This contract will expire shortly. Plants are now in operation at Trail, British Columbia, and at Calgary, Alberta, making ammonia from air.
The third ingredient is sulphuric acid, which is being manufactured from smelter gases given off in the refinement of nickel and copper and from iron pyrites. These sulphuric acid plants are located at Copper Cliff and Valleyfield in the eastern townships.
The fourth item is nitro-glycerin. Glycerin is a by-product obtained in the manufacture of soap. The large soap manufacturers are Procter and Gamble and Lever Brothers. The soap manufacturers make use of domestic animal fats and vegetable oils.
I am advised that the capital cost of the location of this plant at Winnipeg was increased some $500,000 because of the necessity of taking certain material parts there and for other reasons. But the gravamen of the charge against the location at Winnipeg is based on this, that all the product of this

plant has to be transported from Winnipeg
2,000	miles to the seaboard before it can be shipped overseas where it is to be used.

I can answer these questions at once. We have in the department a policy that, as far as possible and reasonable without undue cost, plants will be dispersed out of the industrial areas. This plant was of a type that could be so placed. Naturally, under the present conditions of agriculture in the west, it would be to the advantage of Canada

if we could change over some of the manpower of that section from agriculture to war munitions work.
Two plants have been located. I may say these plants are large users of power and must be located where large blocks of power are available; I think the one in Winnipeg uses some 20,000 horse-power, something of that order. The first plant we located in the Parry Sound area where a large explosives plant had been built during the last war. The second plant we located at De Salaberry island where power and an adequate labour supply were available.
The engineers of the company looked round for available locations for the three plants, and recommendations were made. Perhaps I should not tell the committee; it may get me into trouble, but a location was suggested which would have suited me very much better than the one chosen, as far as I was personally concerned. The Winnipeg location was mentioned. It was definitely felt that it would not be wise to put further explosive plants in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. We had to take into account the fact that practically all the necessary raw material that required transportation in bulk originated west of Winnipeg. There were small quantities perhaps to be brought from the east; I think we have not yet located a plant that did not have some back haul.
The purpose of this explosive plant was primarily to supply the shell-loading plant at Pickering near Toronto, and the movement of materials was a straight line movement towards the seaboard to that plant at Pickering. Of course we locate these shell-loading plants so that we can funnel in all the components that make up the loaded shells without back haul; that is, haul away from the direction that the shell must ultimately travel. As I remember the picture, I think my hon. friend is right in saying that the capital cost at Winnipeg was about $500,000 more than it would have been at De Salaberry. I think, however, he is not correct when he says that the operating costs are higher.

First, I wish to explain why I intervened in order that the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre should have a chance to lay his whole case before this committee. For some days now we have listened to charge after charge, general charges made repeatedly of extravagance, partisanship and so on, without any facts whatever to substantiate them. Days have been so wasted; and although the charges have been answered and answered and the people making them have been asked to bring forward facts in support of them but have been unable to do so, yet the effect has been that the people out in the country are having their confidence shaken to some extent as to the manner in which the war effort is being administered.
If a member of this house brings up a definite, concrete case like this, it seems to me he should be given every opportunity to lay it before parliament, and there should be no attempt to prevent him from doing so. That is particularly true, because of the peculiar nature of the present situation. Ordinarily, if a government department is going to spend money, an appropriation must come before parliament and be granted. In this case, however, a wholly government-owned corporation is spending money, or undertaking to spend money, without that money having-been specifically appropriated. Therefore, if this committee is to do anything other than hold post mortems, we must do exactly what the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre has done; we must lay the facts before the government and ask for the best possible consideration of them before action is finally taken.
What I had intended to say, had I been permitted, was this. I was going to ask the minister not to regard the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre as an attack upon those administering the Allied War Supplies Corporation, and to request that, every time something is questioned in regard to these government-owned corporations, he should not feel called upon to immediately come to their support on the floor of this house. The greatest patriot and hardest working man in the world, even if he works for a dollar a year, may make mistakes. Surely it is the duty of members of this house to bring these matters in all good faith to the attention of the government, which I know desires to see that its agents make as few mistakes as possible. If hon. members are not to be permitted to discharge that duty without being regarded as enemies of the government or as making attacks upon the patriotism of people whom we all admire, then members will be definitely discouraged from doing that which they are sent here to do.
That was why I wished to say a few words in this connection. I am sorry the minister did not let me say a short time ago what I was going to say. I was about to beseech him not to take the attitude that, in fact, at the commencement of his remarks, he did take. I have listened to what has been said by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre. I have no interest in this matter one way or the other, except as a member of this house from Saskatchewan.
If to-day you are actually using or likely to use all the Alberta coal that you can conveniently produce, and if there is an abundance of Saskatchewan coal, then I think the reasons advanced by the minister were insufficient. In all fairness I must admit that. If those reasons are to be accepted as sufficient for over-burdening the industry in Alberta and taking away a demand for what the industry in Saskatchewan can produce, then Saskatchewan might as well make up its mind that it is not going to get anything from the government-owned subsidiaries that have been set up. 1 am bound to say that. No one has greater respect and admiration for the Minister of Munitions and Supply than the member now speaking; I can assure him of that, In season and out of season I have said that, as a member of the government, -he has done a good job for Canada, that he has shown himself to be a good Canadian whom we all admire and respect. I have said that every man in this house should be ready to assist him and should not bother him by carping criticism or general criticism which does nothing but raise doubt and suspicion. When, however, some of the servants or agents of the government
War Appropriation Bill

of this country, servants of the people, of Canada, are suspected of having made a mistake; or, as appears to be the case here, when they may have been too greatly prejudiced by their past connections and may not have carried out the policies of this government, should this government not welcome one of its supporters rising in his place and saying that this man lias perhaps made a mistake; that what he did was in their opinion, not right; that the minister should look into the matter? This should, however, not be done after the action has been taken and the mistake made. I was surprised to read in Hansard this remark by the minister:
If the committee cares to bring down a report to parliament that there has been wasteful expenditure in connection with this installation, I shall be prepared to accept the rebuke and take the responsibility.
No one in this house wants that situation to develop, so that when some servant of this government makes a mistake, the minister, hard-worked as he is, must take the rebuke and the government must take the loss. That is not the way in which parliament should work. If that is all we are going to be able to do here; if we can only hold post mortems and find that money has been lost, and have that constitute a rebuke to a minister, then I submit that we are not discharging the duty which the people have a right to expect of us at this time.
Without prejudice one way or the other I am bound to state that I am not convinced that it would not have been a good thing to instal, in that plant, equipment to burn lignite. The suggestion that this might create dust does not carry weight with me, because I have seen many steam plants established entirely separate from the plants for which they were providing motive power. Of course I am not an engineer, but sitting here as a member of this house, I still think a mistake will be made if equipment is installed to burn bituminous coal, for these reasons: it will be more costly; it will use bituminous coal and overload the producing capacity of Alberta while plenty of Saskatchewan coal is available; it will be more expensive to haul that coal; it will require more labour to get the coal there; it will use and wear out railway equipment when we should economize in every possible way with regard to such equipment.
I realize that the minister is in a difficult position. Unless he stands behind these people, they may throw up their hands and say, "We are not going to work if we are going to be subject to the criticism of every little member of parliament, unless whatever we do, you stand behind us." We all

know the minister's difficulties, and we all sympathize with him; but we also ask him to take into consideration the position in which we, as private members, find ourselves. If there is a suggestion that some mistake has been made, surely it is our duty to draw the matter to his attention. I am convinced that he will consider such suggestions not as attacks upon himself or the government, but rather as attempts to assist in the war effort, about which we are all deeply concerned.

At six o'clock the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) was dealing with the coal situation as it affects western Canada, particularly Saskatchewan. I should like to make a few observations in connection with the discussion which has taken place. I think the minister is altogether too touchy regarding suggestions and comments coming from various parts of the house, and made with a view to having the work of his department more efficient. I think hon. members and the people of the country are convinced that the minister has a most difficult role to fill. In the information which came from the director of public information in to-day's mail there appears a list of the various departments under the supervision of the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe). It is inconceivable that in carrying on the administration of these various departments there should not be some mistakes. I think the people feel that, on the whole, the minister is possibly one of the best qualified men in Canada to administer the affairs of this department.
Many hon. members took the opportunity of seeing some of the work being done. A

War Appropriation Bill
trip of inspection, was arranged by the hon. member for Hamilton East (Mr. Ross) and the citizens of that city. Many of us were able to see the tremendous undertakings which are under way. We saw plans being carried out which will transform the production of ploughshares into the production of guns. We saw great mountains of scrap being transformed into steel. We saw the manufacture of gun barrels. If I remember correctly, these were some twenty-two feet in length and we were able to see them being taken out of huge furnaces and dropped into vats of oil in order to temper the steel. We saw bomb racks under construction and radio equipment being produced, equipment which is so necessary for the carrying on of our war effort. If more hon. members would visit some of these industries, they would be more apt to realize that Canada is really carrying on an important part in the present struggle for the preservation of democracy.
After seeing what is being done in that particular district, I am sure that hon. members feel that the Minister of Munitions and Supply is doing everything humanly possible to see that the work is carried on efficiently. I hope, however, that he will also realize that hon. members are anxious that his work be carried on with as little criticism as possible. It seemed to me that the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre presented a case which should appeal to impartial hon. members. Speaking the other night, he said:
I do know that about eight or nine days ago Mr. Crabtree stated to a colleague of mine in this house that this question was still an open one, that they would approach it with open minds, and yet within thirty-six hours this man Abbott sat in a room in this House of Commons with that same colleague and me and told us that it was a closed book, that it had been closed for months.
Speaking the other day, the minister said:
Mr. Crabtree believes that he would be able to burn a very high percentage of lignite coal in these boilers. I hope that is true, because we are finding it rather difficult to get supplies of bituminous coal from western Canada at the present time. The use of lignite coal at Winnipeg would have a balancing effect upon the coal situation in western Canada. Mr. Crabtree tells me that he will be able to use a considerable portion of lignite coal. He has studied the question, and I have a good deal of confidence in his statement in the matter.
Since the question was raised last week, the minister has had ample opportunity to bring expert opinion to bear upon the matter. Although he spoke at considerable length this afternoon, I still feel that the case made out by the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre stands as a valid one. I should have liked the minister to tell the committee whether, since the question was raised last
week, he had consulted expert opinion or engineers other than those who had given advice to the department on former occasions.
I do not think the objection with respect to the dust creating problem in connection with explosives was well founded. The minister said that they had planned on using a considerable amount of lignite coal; but if they are going to mix lignite with the other coal, there will be a greater dust problem created than if lignite were used exclusively. I would think that the boiler rooms and the place where the coal would be stored would be at a sufficient distance from where the explosives would be made to overcome any great danger from dust that might be created by the use of lignite coal. I should like the minister to tell us who was the technical expert who came with Mr. Crabtree last fall to give him advice, and whether he has secured advice from other engineers since the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre first brought up this question.

I have no brief for Saskatchewan, and I have no intention whatever of entering into an argument as to whether coal should come from Alberta or Saskatchewan. I am definitely of the opinion that there should be a national coal policy, and I believe it is a long time overdue.
The hon. member for Rosthern, who spoke immediately before the supper adjournment, advanced as one of the reasons for using Saskatchewan coal the argument that there should be no attempt to overload the coal industry of Alberta. I assure the hon. member, and other hon. members who are interested, that the coal industry in Alberta is definitely not overburdened. In fact there are hundreds of miners in the Drumheller area who are sitting along the tracks, day after day, with no work to do.
Only a few days ago I read to the house a resolution from that city appealing to the government to do something to relieve the unemployment of employable men in the Drumheller valley. Over 14 per cent of the world's coal deposits are in Alberta, and yet we have hundreds of unemployed men. Just a few days ago I received a memorandum from the coal miners' association in Drumheller showing where the miners in that valley, and in other parts of Alberta, work on an average of only one hundred days in the year, or roughly speaking about one-third of the total time. They have to maintain a living for themselves and their families for the other two-thirds of the year. So certainly one cannot say that the industry is overburdened.
There should be no difficulty getting all the coal required from Alberta, not only to satisfy the requirements of Saskatchewan but for more extensive use here in the eastern and central parts of Canada. War Appropriation Bill

In view of the fact that last year we brought in a tremendous amount of coal from the United States; in view of the fact that this resolution calls for a united effort with regard to our coal problem and asks, in effect, that we form a national coal policy, I think it only right that I should place on record our imports of coal, from a return of the house tabled last year, as follows:

As	I have said before, Mr.	
Chairman, it is difficult to instil patriotism and unity into the people of Canada just by talking, by advertising and by putting out propaganda. If members of the cabinet would spend a little time going among the people, especially in these mining communities, they would find that perhaps these people do not read as much as other classes do; they do not go to as many shows, because they have not the money, to see the expensive propaganda that is shown. They form their opinions from what they see in their daily' life. When they see their people sitting by the side of railroad tracks, unemployed and starving in the midst of the most gigantic war in the history of the world; when they know there will not be enough food on the table for supper, although we are supposed to be in the midst of an all-out war effort, they are not very Teceptive when we say, "You must do your utmost in this war." They look at you in stark amazement and say, "That is exactly what we want to do. Why does the government not let us work?" Here are these able-bodied men, one hundred per cent physically fit; they want to do something. Here we have the city of Drumheller, with its board of trade and even the Liberal organization, which, as I said the other day, sent me a resolution- which was perfectly correct-wanting the government to do something to remedy this condition. And all the time these people know, through their organizations, that last year the government brought in from the United States something more than $48,000,000 worth of coal; and they ask themselves whether the government is really serious about saving foreign exchange. I ask myself that question, too, and I must confess that I have my doubts when I see these things, which I know to be true. One of the most logical and essential things the government should do right at this session is to declare and develop a national coal policy.
As the Minister of Munitions and Supply said a little while ago, and perhaps justly so, this is simply an argument as to whether coal should come from Saskatchewan or Alberta. This simply magnifies the situation and shows the great necessity of a national coal policy for Canada. If we had that, it would have saved much of the argument which has been carried on to-day. Saskatchewan is a nice province; there are nice people there, but they are not quite as nice as the people in Alberta, and their coal is not quite as good. We can supply more coal than they can think of; we can supply all Canada with coal, and I am not overlooking the tremendous amount of coal available in Nova Scotia and eastern Canada. They have problems there which should be given consideration. As I say, all this simply magnifies the fact that the Department of Munitions and Supply or the appropriate department should get together and form and announce a national coal policy for Canada.

speechtext:
During the passage of this resolution through the committee, the Minister of Munitions and Supply has attempted to explain the bottle-necks which exist in aircraft, shipbuilding production and other industries by outlining the difficulty the government has in obtaining skilled labour. I should like to ask the Minister of Munitions and Supply and the Minister of National War Services just what collaboration there is between the two departments. We understood that the National Resources Mobilization Act was passed last year for the purpose of tabulating all the available labour resources in Canada, in order to classify them into categories and to move men or give them assistance in moving so that they might be able to contribute to a maximum war effort. Could either of the ministers involved give the committee a statement as to what collaboration has taken place between the two departments?
A national volunteer registration bureau was set up in the Department of National
War Appropriation Bill

War Services and a national registration was held last year. The only value of such a registration is to permit the government to find skilled labour in shipbuilding, skilled technicians, men and women who are experienced in explosive manufacturing, and other types of labour. I have a case in mind, and perhaps other hon. members could duplicate it. I have received letters from people who are working on farms but who had experience in the manufacture of high explosives during the last war. In every case I have turned the name over to officials in the Department of Munitions and Supply. These are people who possess some skilled knowledge in this particular industry and who are desirous of making what contribution they can toward Canada's war effort.
That, however, is not enough. About nine months ago the government set itself the task of taking an inventory of the labour resources of Canada. What has been done about it? What results have been obtained? A few days ago I had on the order paper a question about this, and the answer I received was that the only figures compiled so far were for Ontario. How soon will the figures for the other provinces be compiled? How soon will the Department of National War Services be able to say to the Department of Munitions and Supply that they know where technicians are available and can give it names and addresses?
Under the Department of Labour young men are being trained with a view to absorbing them into war industry. Only last evening I had in my office a young man who had just come from Toronto. Previously he had lived in the west, but he had come to Toronto to take an eight weeks' training course at Danforth technical school. Along with the rest of his class he had graduated as a machinist, but all these young men find there are no jobs for them. When they started the course they were told that jobs would be available before they were finished, that they might not be able to complete the course. When, however, they finished the course there were no jobs. They were told to go and see the Massey-Harris people, but when they went there they were advised that 150 men had been laid off and these men would have first claim on any jobs. This young man told me they went to the John Inglis company where they were told that 50 men had been recently laid off and would be given first call before any new men were taken on.
There is something wrong. We have been told that there is a scarcity of technicians and skilled labour; we have been told frequently by the Minister of Labour that

we are going to need 200,000 or 300,000 skilled men. Those statements do not jibe with the experiences of these young men who have taken these courses and who find they cannot get jobs, although the very thing the government has been training them for is to enable them to undertake work in war industry. There is no use in the government spending money to train young men and then have them go back to the farm.
I think the committee would appreciate an explanation from either one of the ministers involved. We should like to know what steps have been taken to mobilize labour, to find out where qualified technical men can be obtained, of whom the Minister of Munitions and Supply says there is a scarcity. We wish to know where these men can be located and what steps are being taken to place them.

speechtext:
I have not before me at the moment the statistics from which I could give this information. During the last two or three weeks we have been going round in circles as far as the discussion is concerned, and it is difficult to have material available at all times. All the questions which were asked during the last few moments were answered a few days ago and the answers now appear in Hansard. The figures with regard to Ontario, as well as the general statistics with regard to all Canada, were given. The statement was made that in another week or ten days the figures with regard to the other provinces would be available. They can be very closely estimated from the Ontario figures. As far as the registration is concerned, hon. members know that this was started in August of last year, being completed on August 22. Immediately afterwards a compilation was begun of the statistics gathered through that registration.
I may say that from time to time certain information has been passed on to different industries in Canada as well as to the Department of Labour. Any information required by the Department of Munitions and Supply respecting certain types of labour that might be available in certain places has been passed on from time to time. Last night some reference was made to a number of young men who have gone over to Great Britain from Canada to take part in the operation of the instruments made available for the purpose of locating planes at night and in connection with night flying. Practically all of those young men were located through the registration. The first 1,500 were located in one city. Their names were handed to the officials who visited the homes of those men house by house, and they were

War Appropriation Bill
on their way to Great Britain in a very short time. The registration figures are being made use of in that way from time to time.
One of the difficulties that we experience in connection with the matter is the fact that nearly every one who applies for employment applies, in the first instance, to the wrong place. Over a long term of years it has been customary for persons who were looking for employment to make application at the employment offices across Canada. For some reason or another, however, a great many people now think they should make application to Ottawa and they write to some minister or to some person connected with the promotion of some particular industry. We simply had to advise them that all the information with regard to these matters is now, as it always has been, at the labour offices and that that is the proper place to apply; that they can get action quicker in that way than by applying to someone else somewhere else. With that information sent back to them, some of them do find it possible to locate employment.
I quite realize that not all of those who desire employment in different parts of Canada have been brought into contact with industry that requires their labour. We have some difficulty in bringing that about, difficulties sometimes associated with the place where the person is now living and the circumstances under which he has been living. Sometimes it is difficult to take the head of the family away from the family, and sometimes it is difficult to move the whole family. There are all kinds of inconveniences of that sort because of the great distances in this country, but we are trying to work out methods of dealing with these different problems that arise. There have been advertisements from time to time put in the western papers seeking applications from persons who are competent to do certain kinds of work, such as shipbuilding, requesting them to apply for jobs in other parts of Canada, and by that method many of those who require work have been brought into contact with employment.
I do not know just how soon we shall have all the figures in connection with the registration, but I am informed by the members of the staff in the statistics branch that the figures will practically all be ready before the end of this month.

I cannot give a categorical answer as to the definite percentage placed of those who have taken training courses. We are operating training courses at a substantially high rate at the present time. It is regrettable, but it is a fact that in certain localities some of those who have received training have not yet been placed. For example, a situation arose last fall where we had something like 500 men in Calgary who had received upwards of 600 hours of training, and who did not have employment. We arranged to transport them to a point where there was employment, and I think it is not unfair to say that all those 500 men were placed in employment. It undoubtedly is true that we are training faster in certain localities than the war industries in that particular locality can take care of the men. It is necessary to arrange for their transpor-
War Appropriation Bill

tation, and even when that is done, you are going to find the isolated case of a man who cannot immediately secure employment.
Let me give to the hon. member the figures, which are quite recent, of the number of trainees in the month of February; that is, the number receiving training in that month. There are four branches of training being carried on under the general training plan of the government. There are, first of all, the war emergency classes; there are the war industrial classes, under the youth training programme; there are the army classes, under the war emergency training programme; then there are the Royal Canadian Air Force classes, training aeroplane mechanics and those who are to take their place in the aircraft manufacturing industry.
In February, the month just past, we had in training in the war emergency classes, 6.351; in the war industrial classes, under the youth training programme, 992; in the army classes, under the war emergency training programme, 2,353; and in the Royal Canadian Air Force classes, training aeroplane mechanics and those who will be engaged in aircraft manufacturing, 1,727; or a total throughout Canada of 11,423. That was the number of trainees whom we were training in the month of February.
Please do not get an incorrect impression from that. It does not follow that that number joined the training classes in the month of February or that they were turned out in the month of February. That is the total number of trainees in that month.
Then as to the average time for training, the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) mentioned eight weeks. That is substantially below the average.

Generally speaking, I
think it will be correct to say that the average is about three months. Mind you, in dealing with the number trained, we do not deal with those who go into industrial plants and perhaps spend seven or eight days in learning a trade. They are not included in these figures. I think I am safe in saying that the average period of training-in some instances it may be longer and, in some instances, shorter-is three months; we have 11,423 men in training in one month, and the number is constantly increasing. That was the number in training in February. In January the equivalent figure of the total number of trainees was 10,381. In other words, February increased over January, in the number of those receiving training during the month, by over 1,000.

I have that figure somewhere, but it does not appear to be right at hand; I shall be glad to give it to my hon. friend. In a rough way I suppose you could calculate it. If the average period of training is three months, and there were 11,000 in training in the month, there would be a present output of over 3,000 a month, but I shall be glad to supply the hon. member with the exact figure because we have it.
That is the situation, scattered throughout Canada. Then vocational training is carried on in seventy-five schools situated in different parts of Canada. In some of those parts, war industry is carrying on at a tremendous rate; in others, though having the advantage of trainees, war industry is not so substantially located. It is inevitable that between the time of training and the time of securing employment, some delay occurs. What we are endeavouring to do in connection with the training programme-and I am dealing now only with vocational training, to which I assume the hon. member for Weyburn referred -is to stimulate the use of vocational schools. I hope by the time this measure is through to have a somewhat complete report as to the success which has been obtained in plant schools.
We are, however, endeavouring to attain a condition in which those who receive training will not have to return, as the hon. member remarked, to territories where industrial concentration is not great. We are trying to correlate the training plan with industry itself so that, once a man receives his training, he will, as soon as possible, be placed. As the Minister of Munitions and Supply pointed out, we are up against a difficulty as to individual characteristics of the particular trainee. That is inevitable. We shall be faced with the difficulty that you cannot secure immediate employment for those who are trained. But we believe that, when this general industrial movement reaches its height, there will be employment for every trainee whom we can turn out; in fact our difficulty at that time will be to provide enough trainees.

Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to take up much of the time of the committee; I feel that we are getting pretty well tired of the discussion. But you recall that on Friday evening, at the closing hour, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) tried to leave with the country and the committee certain impressions respecting the purchase of lumber for the Debert camp. These I gathered under the following headings:

War Appropriation Bill
1.	That a large portion of the lumber used in construction at Debert military camp was purchased from Harry J. Mackenzie at very high prices.
2.	That H. J. Mackenzie was my campaign manager during the March, 1940, election.
3.	That a portion of my lumber was included in the Mackenzie sale.
4.	That Mackenzie, an insurance agent, was not previously interested in the lumber business.
On Monday, the Minister of National Defence pointed out that the lumber sold by Mackenzie was about one per cent of the total amount comprised in the purchase. He further showed that the price paid to Mackenzie was very reasonable.
At the time the discussion was on, I denied that Harry Mackenzie was my campaign manager. I do not propose to say who my manager was, but I think a good many hon. gentlemen here will say that, whoever he was, he made a fairly good job of it.
That a portion of my lumber was included in the Mackenzie sale I denied at that time.
We come now to the statement of the leader of the opposition with respect to Harry J. Mackenzie not having been previously interested in the lumber business. This evening at around six o'clock the following telegram reached my desk:
Have been interested in lumber at various times for thirty years. Did not solicit orders for Debert. Was called to hotel by Mr. McCabe and asked if I could supply special sizes which I had on hand. Standard price delivered at Debert. Will have one million feet of first class lumber for delivery early summer at competitive prices. Will go to Ottawa at Hanson's expense if necessary. Letter to follow.
H. J. Mackenzie.
Now that we have laid the last wrinkle in the shroud of the ghost raised by the leader of the opposition, I do not think I should say anything more, except, in closing, to leave the idea that it does seem a shame that because a known Liberal gets a contract from the government it is immediately suggested around the country that there is something underhand about it, and that he is making money at the expense of the country.
You know, sir, that in this chamber there are some big big men, and there are some big little men, and there are some little little men and there are some little big men. I am going to leave it with you and the committee and the country just where the leader of the opposition places himself by making such an unwarranted reflection upon a friend and follower of mine.

I realize, as I think all hon. members must, the magnitude of the work which the government has to do, to organize in eighteen months all the activities which have been necessary because of the war, and there are bound to be some complaints, a number of bottlenecks, and a certain amount of disorganization. In the western cities, however, there is a great deal of unemployment. I made inquiries of the city hall in Vancouver by letter a few days ago, and I am told that there are at present over 10,000 unemployed, of whom over 7,000 are employable. I should be very glad to adopt the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver East. A survey is now proceeding in connection with the plant schools. May I, however, point out to the committee that there are two phases of the work which the interdepartmental committee on labour supply is doing. One is through the vocational schools, and the special training schools for aeroplane mechanics. Another phase of it deals with an entirely different matter, namely the plant schools. It is a little difficult to get exact information as to the volume of training being done in the latter schools. The survey is, however, now under way, and I believe that within a few days it will give us a more accurate picture.
I appreciate what the hon. member for Vancouver East has said with regard to the situation in Vancouver. It is, I know, a little different from any other city in Canada, and necessarily so, on account of the charming climate of British Columbia and the city of Vancouver in the winter time; and the figures he gives are not startling.
Generally speaking, I am advised by the officials in British Columbia, they are largely those of unskilled labour, and there is a period of definite seasonal unemployment at that point. Perhaps the situation is more aggravated in Vancouver than in any other city. I believe that to be fair.
I shall be very glad, when the bill is in committee, to give a complete statement of the whole training plan. I have given figures indicating that the plan as regards adoption
War Appropriation Bill

of industrial training classes in the development of aeroplane mechanics and air training mechanics is operating in a pretty substantial way. I should like to be able to give to the committee definite figures of the plant schools.
Generally speaking, the plan is to train in the coming year 1941-I speak of the calendar year-something over 100,000 men. It is designed that about 80,000 of these will be available to war industries, and as far as basic training is concerned they will be skilled men. I do not suggest that after they go through basic training they do not also have to take certain practical training in the plants. The members of the committee will agree that that is essential, but, generally speaking, we aim through the plant schools, the training schools, to train not less than 100,000 men this calendar year. I shall be glad to give a break-down of the figures when the bill is in committee, if that is satisfactory to hon. members.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Northumberland has produced many famous men. If not by birth, certainly by environment, we produced the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett. I would refer also to Lord Beaver-brook, to whom the eyes of the world look for assistance in this terrific struggle. Northumberland had the distinction of having two fathers of confederation, an outstanding historical event.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Cumberland had four.
Mr. O'BRIEN:	Probably Cumberland
needed four as against Northumberland's two. I do not want to take up the time of the committee with historical references, but I should like to refer to an old member from that county. Mr. W. S. Loggie is now ninety-one years old, taking an active interest in present day events. He was speaking in this house when the House of Commons caught fire in 1916. I hope that no similar disaster occurs at this moment.
To get down to the matter of shipbuilding, the reason why I am now on my feet, I do not wish to be considered as wailing over the conditions which prevail in Northumberland county. We consider ourselves to be rugged individualists, and we and our forefathers have always tried to maintain ourselves without applying to other governmental bodies for assistance. On May 26, 1866, our forefathers went to the polls with high hopes in their hearts. As I speak here to-night I wonder whether those high hopes have been fulfilled. I should like to place on record some information contained in the submission by the municipality of Northumberland to the royal commission on dominion-provincial relations. Quoting from page 9, I read:
There is a great deal of unemployment and much poverty in the county. Perhaps it is this increase in unemployment and poverty that has given the marked increase in tuberculosis and insanity.
The assistance to the poor is a parish affair and as little outside relief as possible is given.
And again:
Certain obligations and services now performed by the municipality should be taken over by the province or the dominion or at least there should be a greater contribution therefor paid to the municipality by the province or the dominion or both.
That submission was made prior to the war. One might believe that in an all-out war effort similar conditions could not prevail, indeed could not be foreseen at this time. I hope it may not be thought that while we sit in this committee pondering national problems, my references may seem to be parochial. I represent this constituency and my constituents look to me for some measure

of help and assistance. In 1932 the gross bonded debt of the municipality was only 842,000, with $22,269 of a sinking fund, leaving a net debt of only $19,730. The final figures quoted in this submission are for 1937, by which date the gross debt of $42,000 had multiplied exactly ten times in five years and stood at $420,000. In the intervening years since 1937, the debt has reached the astounding sum of very close to $600,000, largely due to the years of depression and the severe and difficult times through which that municipality passed.
To explain the situation fairly to this committee would take too long a time and would be too involved a matter. I have no intention of doing so, but I should like to cite from the submission that paragraph which says:
The conclusion that unemployment has become a national problem and should be dealt with as such is rather obvious. We submit that the matter of unemployment relief has grown to such proportions that it has long since ceased to be a subject of local or private interest and has become one of national concern.
As I said, that was pre-war, pre-September, 1939. Since then, money has been expended at such a terrific rate that perhaps even the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley)-and I say this not unkindly-has not been able to keep up with the terrific pace because through no fault of his own, after bringing down this resolution asking the house to appropriate $1,300,000,000 for war expenditures only a few days later he announced that $160,000,000 more was required. And so the expenditure goes on at this terrific rate. Yet the municipality of Northumberland, after passing through the most severe years of the depression to which I have referred, now finds itself-I hope I am not prophesying that which may happen, but I cannot see any other outcome-entering upon what we believe will be another period of depression, because the constituency which I represent depends largely upon fishing, and particularly upon lumbering.
Prior to the war we were making shipments to Europe, to a country which I would not in present circumstances care to mention as being that country upon which our people had to depend for their livelihood and sustenance. That is perhaps a travesty upon what we call our democracy and perhaps upon our commonwealth of nations. That, however, is in the past, and I hope that when peace is declared, such conditions may not prevail again.
Realizing as I do that in times of war we must submit ourselves and our desires to the overwhelming demands of the war effort and that people in various localities throughout Canada must suffer to a certain degree, never-

War Appropriation Bill
theless with a view to alleviating the possible, perhaps probable suffering in the constituency I represent, I plead with the government to attempt to do something, within the scope of the war effort, for the people of my constituency, and it might perhaps be shipbuilding. That has been referred to by hon. members from Nova Scotia, where shipbuilding has been carried on more extensively in recent years. The Miramichi has a wonderful history of shipbuilding dating back to 1796, when ships were first built there and pine masts were shipped across the Atlantic for his majesty's navy. From that time down until 1860 or 1875 we were building ships there. True, we have not built any ships in recent years, although we built one sailing ship during the last war. The Minister of Munitions and Supply, and perhaps rightly so from the point of view of budgeting and watching the national purse as we believe at least the national purse should be watched, has not so far done anything in approximating volume for us in the maritimes, in shipbuilding, maybe because we have not the trained men. I admit that we have not the trained men in Miramichi, but I submit that if we have not these men already trained, they at least are there and it is our duty to attempt to train them so that they may be enabled to earn their livelihood.
Seventy-five years ago, Mr. Chairman, we did not have a Dominion of Canada, and eighteen months ago we did not have a Department of Munitions and Supply. All these things have been created because of the necessity of the moment. Now that the timber controller in the United Kingdom has stopped the purchases of our lumber-I hoped at first that this would be but a temporary measure, but now I believe that it will be permanent-with that in the offing, the people of Northumberland county are faced with the prospect of going through this summer and into next winter with virtually nothing to do in the way of earning the living to which they are entitled. Therefore, I plead with the minister, yes, with the ministry, to see if he or they cannot possibly do something for the people of my constituency.
We hear a great deal these days that we must "stick to fundamentals"; but when one asks what these fundamentals are, no definite answer is given. The only fundamental I know, pre-war, and the only reason for having government and for having these houses of parliament, is to create some degree of happiness so that the people for whom we legislate may be able to live, not in luxury necessarily, but at least in happiness and contentment.
Since the war broke out, the one overwhelming fundamental is the winning of the war. If, however, our finances have in some way become so tangled that we must pay tribute to an inanimate thing called gold; if human happiness must circulate about that gold standard, we have perhaps reached the point where it has ceased to be of any useful value in the lives of the ordinary citizens.
I know little about financial problems in the higher involved order, and I have met very few others who seem to know just what it all means; but I do maintain that at the present time-I hope I am wrong-the dollar sign seems to be the guiding factor, and in Canada the dollar sign seems to be almost placed upon the glorious union jack. That, I think, we dare not have. If the people of Britain need our products of the maritimes; if they need ships, then in this fight to save democracy and civilization we should give everything we possibly can even if we must do it "on the cuff", as a matter of credit. It seems strange to me that we here in Canada, directly connected with and a part of the British empire, should find our cousins to the south virtually giving to that empire in order to save those things in which the people of the United States believe, while we here in Canada apparently cannot do that, but must have Canadian dollars of which Britain is now running short.
These matters are all too involved for me to attempt to solve them or even to explain them because, after all, I am only thinking out loud, which is what I believe most members of the house are doing. Yet perhaps in thinking out loud we may arrive at some possible solution that would be of benefit not only to the people of my constituency to whom I am responsible but to the whole dominion. Therefore, so long as I occupy this seat in this house, I dedicate myself and this seat to the service of the government, not in any maudlin way that would assume the government to be letter perfect in everything they do, but rather in a constructive sense. It is for that reason I have until now refrained from taking up the time of the house in making what I think have been perhaps somewhat neutral speeches. Again I dedicate myself and my seat to the members of the government individually and collectively so that, as a unit in the constitutional government of this country, I, during my tenure of office, may satisfy at least myself that I have done what I think is the decent thing.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The hon. member for Cumberland raised somewhat the same question as was raised last week by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg.
IFar Appropriation Bill

As far as the building of ships in Nova Scotia is concerned, there was only one firm in Nova Scotia at the beginning of the war, and I think there is only one now, that would undertake the building of steel ships, namely, the Halifax Shipyards, Limited. Nobody else in that province was equipped to build steel ships, but this firm could have built mine-sweepers or ships as large as 10,000 tons. It was felt, however, that they could better devote their energies to the repairing of ships, and they have been very busily engaged in that work since the beginning of the war. In New Brunswick the Saint John Dry Dock company or a subsidiary have now the contract for the building of three corvettes, and they also have a good deal of repair work.
At that time, no other yards in either province could undertake the building of a steel ship of any size, and up to the present the policy of the government has not been to bonus or subsidize shipyards, in view of the fact that there are at the present time and were at the beginning of the war fifteen or sixteen or perhaps twenty yards in Canada which could undertake the building of steel ships.
After I came to Ottawa I had many requests from Nova Scotia asking money from the government for the repair or establishment of shipyards for the construction of wooden ships, or perhaps, steel ships. Obviously it would be rather unfair to existing yards which have been developed by private capital for the government to go in and erect government yards when there were enough existing yards in the country to carry on such work as was available.
With regard to wooden ships, I have given my hon. friend some figures indicating that orders were placed in Nova Scotia for some 126 wooden ships. They were mostly small ships, but there were two classes for which orders were placed a few months ago, many of which I hoped, would be built in Nova Scotia. These were the Fairmile boats, the motor launches 112 feet long, and the wooden mine-sweepers.
To show that every effort was made to get Nova Scotian builders into the production of wooden ships, I may say that my colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply sent down last August the director of shipbuilding, Mr. Carswell, who surveyed all the shipyards in the east before the orders for these wooden ships were placed. It seems to me that if the Nova Scotian builders, in view of the fact that twenty-four ships were to be ordered in the Fairmile plant, had wanted the work, and if their bids had been low

enough, they could easily have got eighteen or twenty, because there is no question that my hon. friend is right when he says that the proportion of money going to Nova Scotia for shipbuilding is very small as compared with the sums which have gone to Quebec, Ontario or British Columbia. It is out of proportion in relation to a great shipbuilding province such as Nova Scotia. Therefore it was the desire of my colleague the Minister of Munitions and Supply, and, the hon. member for Cumberland will agree, it was my desire to see perhaps eighteen or twenty of these Fairmile boats built in Nova Scotia. That would have meant orders amounting to something like a million and a half dollars for the wooden shipyards of that province. What happened?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: : The Fairmile ships of which the minister is speaking are mahogany ships, are they not?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Mahogany planking and so forth, yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
