No; it is a little less than that. It is something around $90,000 for the hull. It is under $100,000; I have not the exact figures here.
Mr. Carswell went down to Nova Scotia, looked at the yards, and discovered that there were a good many which were capable of building the ships. Tenders were invited from those yards; the government of Nova Scotia interested itself in the matter, called a meeting of the shipbuilders, urged them to go on; called a second meeting of the shipbuilders, sent to Ottawa a delegation of shipbuilders accompanied by a minister of the crown in Nova Scotia; but after all that work the only Nova Scotian tender which was at all comparable with tenders from Ontario and British Columbia in the matter of wooden ships was one by a man at Weymouth, who tendered for and received a contract for two ships.
Mr. Mac*NICOL: At what price?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Only three other tenders were received, and none of them was at all within the mark. That is the Fairmile story.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
On that matter of tenders, would the minister make this clear: how did the Nova Scotia tenders compare with others, and what is the reason for the tenders from Nova Scotia being higher? A desire for more profits? How does the minister explain such a difference?

ll'ar Appropriation Bill

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Well, I do not know. All I know is that the government of Nova Scotia urged these people to get their tenders down as low as possible, because we knew the competition would be stiff. These people had plenty of time to consider the plans; indeed, they were given extensions of time for that purpose. In spite of that, there was only one man who could meet the price advanced by builders in British Columbia and Ontario. What the reason is I do not know.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Is not the reason that, so far as Ontario is concerned, a great number of boats of this type are in use, and large numbers are made, in the counties of Mus-koka and Parry Sound and Midland, and towns adjacent to Georgian bay? That is where these classes of boats are used.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: Yes; there is a good deal of that sort of building Tound the Georgian bay district and Midland, but that does not answer the question of the hon. member for Cape Breton South.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: British Columbia pays the highest wage.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
British Columbia pays a high wage. Of course there are firms in that province which have done a great deal of shipbuilding in recent years. They have splendid timber, and for some reason or another they are able to underbid Nova Scotians for the construction of these ships.
The next type of wooden ship, in size, which we had to build was the mine-sweeper. Eight of these mine-sweepers were for the British Admiralty and were built to their specifications. It is true the specifications called for expensive woods, such as teak, which Nova Scotia people were not entirely accustomed to, but neither, I suppose, were the builders in other parts of Canada. Every Nova Scotian builder of any consequence was given a chance to bid on these mine-sweepers. I have here a list of twelve builders who were asked to bid and who did bid. The first eight of these British ships-the whole eight-were awarded to Nova Scotia. What has happened? Four builders have renounced their contracts. They have said that they will not go on with the contracts to build these ships because, as they are honest enough to admit, they do not think they can do it for the money in the time specified, and they have asked to be released. That is the story with regard to the minesweepers.
Everything possible has been done. I should think, in fairness to the builders in that province, both by the authorities here and by
the government of Nova Scotia, but there is an unfortunate condition. It may be, as my hon. friend pointed out, that the builders there, accustomed to working on a small scale, have not the necessary capital. It may be that when they saw the expensive wood that would be required, such as mahogany and teak, which will have to be imported and paid for, they felt that they had not the capital necessary to undertake the work. Whatever the reason may be, there is the result. It is unfortunate, but I do not see that anything more could have been done here.
One other word. My hon. friend said he thought the matter of shipping was second in importance only to aircraft and aircraft production. It is my judgment that it is second to nothing at all in the winning of the war. So long as Britain remains an island and so long as she has to get supplies from overseas, shipping and the protection of shipping will be absolutely vital to the life of that country. There is no question in the world about it. We must have not only cargo ships to carry supplies to England but ships of other kinds which are just as necessary-underwater craft, surface craft and, at other stages, aircraft for purposes of protection.
That brings me to this point. You cannot take a navy, whether it be a merchant navy or a service navy, and turn out its ships and its men overnight. This afternoon I was pondering the time it takes to train an officer in the navy. Someone has asked how many men were promoted from the ranks, and what educational qualifications were required. I believe I told the hon. member for Vancouver East that at least senior matriculation was required for entrance into the Royal Canadian Navy, but after that a cadet would have to go to naval college at Dartmouth, England- I am talking of peace time-for a period of about two years. He would then be made a midshipman and be at sea for about a year and six months or two years more. Then he would be a sub-lieutenant for a year and a half or two years more. He would then take some courses of about six months to qualify as lieutenant. At the end of six years of study, after he had acquired matriculation standing, he would be a lieutenant in the navy. At the end of another eight years he would be a lieutenant commander. Thereafter his promotion would depend on merit and selection.
You cannot turn out such men overnight, nor can you turn out skilled shipbuilders overnight. The thing to remember in this house in future is, I think, that whatever you may be able to do in other respects, and without in any way attempting to depreciate the importance of other services, the naval service is one the nucleus of which, both in
War Appropriation Bill

service personnel and in shipbuilding personnel, should never be allowed to decrease below the danger point. It has been allowed to decrease below that point here and in other countries as well in the last twenty years, and this and other countries are feeling the effect to-day.
We are trying our best to train men for the navy to man the ships we are building, and it is not an easy task in view of the high calibre of training required in a naval officer or even a petty officer. As regards the shipyards of the country, the programme which was agreed to in 1939 for shipbuilding in Canada, estimated at four years, is going to be compressed into the space of two and a half years. Every ship that we planned to build up to the year 1943 will have been completed in 1942.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: But not destroyers?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: No, because the plan had not contemplated destroyers. I am speaking of the plan made in 1939 on the basis of what was then considered to be the capacity of Canadian yards. We said that we could build so many corvettes, mine-sweepers and patrol boats; that was all that we could do, and the plan was to last until the end of 1943. That plan will be completed next year owing-I think it is fair to say-to the enterprise, courage, skill and energy of the shipbuilders of the country who have done a magnificent bit of work in this regard.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
Accepting the statement of the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services, that the building and maintenance in operation of ships constitutes the most important of our war activities, and accepting the assurance of the Minister of Munitions and Supply that he is endeavouring to harness the shipbuilding capacity and the man-power of Canada to its utmost, I feel that some special effort should be put forward to get the production that can be derived from Nova Scotia and New Brunswick. I am satisfied that if proper efforts are made, a very much increased programme of production can be obtained in Nova Scotia. I am of opinion that the time has come when the yards and the facilities and the men should be subsidized and encouraged in order that the shipbuilding programme can be pressed to its utmost limit, and I should hope that the Minister of National Defence for Naval Services and the Minister of Munitions and Supply would make special efforts to this end.
I was surprised to see the following Canadian Press dispatch from Shelburne, Nova Scotia, yesterday, showing that this yard has no construction work. I quote:

Shelburne, Nova Scotia, March 16	(C.P.)
The 118-foot freighter U.K. service IV was launched Saturday from the ship yard of Winslow Mack-ay Sons Limited and shortly after that officials of the company announced they were closing down the yards for lack of further orders. The 149-ton wooden vessel built for a firm at LaHave, N.S. was the 14th turned out by the plant in the last year.
We accept this as correct, coming from the Canadian Press. It seems to me that with the present need for the building of ships, this condition should not exist. There should be officials from the Department of National Defence for Naval Services and the Department of Munitions and Supply following up the work in these yards, to see that new construction is offered to them to the limit of their capaoity. Not only should the yards be given business to the limit of their present capacity, but they should be expanded, as has been done in connection with munitions factories, largely in central Canada. I suggest there should be some explanation as to why a dispatch such as I have quoted' should be sent across Canada at a time like this, when there is such pressing need for more ships of many kinds.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext: I had intended to deal with that matter when I spoke earlier, but it slipped my mind. The hon. member has referred to the shipyards of Winslow Mackay Sons Limited at Shelburne. I would reply that the Mackay company were asked to tender on the Fairmiles, but did not put in a bid. That happened last fall. They were again asked to bid on the mine-sweepers. They said they would not bid on that type of boat, but they might be interested in a somewhat similar type of boat built on Canadian designs and of Canadian material. The Mackay company has had some work from the government, although not a great amount. I believe it has built three derrick scows, four float scows, and four wooden lighter skids, but it has not bid on the larger wooden ships.

speechtext:
I wonder whether it would not be possible to-morrow for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) to give a full statement of the representations which have been made regarding the repatriation of funds. Something was said about it in the press. There is now a mission, and I believe most of the work is done by one missionary, Sir Edward Peacock, who is now in the United States, selling British capital.
Besides the statement about repatriation, I should like to know if Sir Edward will come to Canada on the same mission, and if part of his mission is to sell the stock of the Canadian Pacific Railway to the Canadian government. I am more interested in it because Sir Edward himself is a director of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and all the
movement behind a union government converges on the amalgamation of railways.
In addition to that, it would be interesting to see the connection of the Hon. Charles Dunning with the directors of the Canadian Pacific Railway, showing the boards on which he sits with the directors of that railway. All that is done behind the stage, and we, of course, need information about it.
I remember reading in the press some months ago a statement about the repatriation of funds for the Grand Trunk Railway. The question was not decided for a long time; but finally some pressure was brought to bear, and a decision was reached regarding the repatriation of those funds. These are general questions, and I can understand that it would be impossible for the minister to answer them to-night. I shall be pleased, however, if he would look at Hansard to-morrow, and see what he can do about giving an answer.
People are ready to make sacrifices for war, but the question is as to what is properly called war. It is most absurd to think that the Canadian people will suffer privation to increase the value of the stock of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and to give some schemers an opportunity to make much more money at the expense of our people. The feeling in Canada is strongly against amalgamation of the railways. Those who are for it do not come out boldly; they try to get it in some other way, in a different way from that to which we are accustomed. The purpose of the last union government was not to win the war; the railway business was behind it, and now there is another railway scheme behind the move for a union government. That is known by everyone. We want some enlightenment on the matter. I do not wish to take the minister by surprise. I respect and admire him, but the matter is of such tremendous importance that we are entitled to full information about it, which I hope the minister will be kind enough to supply. I am not making any attack on Mr. Dunning, although it would be very easy for me to k.o. him. I am just asking for facts. The matter is so serious, so important, that we should not show false sympathy to anyone who is behind the curtain.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
The hon. member for
Simcoe North is behind the curtain.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR GRANTING TO HIS MAJESTY AID FOR NATIONAL DEFENCE AND SECURITY
speechtext:
He is there, but he is not offensive.
There is another matter that should be investigated as well; that is, the Purvis business, the C.I.L. We must have full light on the C.I.L. and all the interlocking companies. After the Minister of Finance has answered
War Appropriation Bill

those questions, with regard to the amalgamation of the railways and Mr. Dunning's connections with the Canadian Pacific Railway, and so on, I shall have other and more interesting questions to ask the Minister of Munitions and Supply. But everything in good time; I am not in a rush. We are here to take our time, to judge the pros and cons of everything. I am not acting in any spirit of animosity.
Let me add one further word. Last year when I mentioned to the leader of the official opposition that some people were receiving large fees and high salaries, some members of the Conservative party protested vehemently, and the leader of the opposition said he had resigned all his directorships when he was appointed leader of his party. According to Hansard, however, he has kept at least one, and in a guide in the library it is stated that he has several others. I do not object to that at all, but what is interesting is the connection between a man who is a director of a company and other men who are directors of the same company and who sometimes may confuse their private interests with public interest, unless they are great enough completely to sacrifice their private interests and think only of the public interest. That would be praiseworthy, but I am not yet sure that it applies in this case. I do not say that it does not apply; I am very careful, and I want to use parliamentary language. After I get the information about Mr. Dunning, I will show the business connections of the leader of the opposition, and then I will go further and show what are the jobs of those whom he defends in this house. Then people will have all the information. I do not say there is anything evil in that, but the people should have full information before we vote such amounts of money as we are asked to vote now.
There is only one further observation I wish to make. If the Minister of Finance is able to collect the amount called for in this measure, he will be the best man ever born in Canada. I know he is a good man, but we have to be very careful. Some people say, "Oh, let it go." The duty of the opposition is not to step on it but to apply the brake at times, but this the leader of the opposition never does. We have to apply the brakes from this side. I am afraid, Mr. Chairman, that if we go too far, if we become careless or reckless, the result will be that we shall have to go to the United States for money, and if we have to do that, my great fear is annexation in the near future. I fear it very deeply. I want Canada to remain a British dominion, and my constituents and I are

ready to make great sacrifices in order that this may be so. We desire to be at peace with the United States, who are our allies. We want to keep them as our allies, because their interests are the same as ours in this war. On the other hand we do not want annexation at any time; and if we have to go to the United States to borrow huge sums of money, annexation will be all the closer. That is a matter to consider. I do not want to be a false prophet, but I tell the committee frankly what I think about the matter.
